summary: This RFC defines multipart/report, a MIME media type serving as a general container for email reports of any kind. It is described here only for delivery status reports, but one type for all reports helps mail software. It is on the standards track and obsoletes RFC 3462.

eli5.summary: An envelope that holds a note and extra papers together. Mail systems use it to bundle a message saying that delivery failed, along with the details.

questions: what is a delivery status report container
subtitle: The MIME container that wraps a mail system report: a human note, a machine-readable account and, optionally, the original message.

tldr.problem: The earlier definition of multipart/report could be used only as the outermost MIME type of a message, which blocked sending several reports in one message or forwarding a report inside another multipart message.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6522 keeps the media type as it was, a container of two or three body parts in a fixed order, removes the outermost-only constraint, and also defines the text/rfc822-headers type for returning just a message's header.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 3462, which is now Historic along with its predecessor RFC 1892, and is an Internet Standard that has since been updated by RFC 6533.

today: RFC 6522 is an Internet Standard and obsoletes RFC 3462, which, with its predecessor RFC 1892, is marked Historic. It has been updated by RFC 6533.

sections.title: Why This Update Exists
sections.content:
multipart/report is a MIME media type that acts as a container for mail system administrative reports of various kinds. RFC 3462 and its predecessor declared it, but required it to be used only as the outermost MIME type of a message.

Practical experience showed that this was overly restrictive. It limited the transmission of multiple administrative reports within a single overall message container, and it prevented forwarding a report as part of another multipart MIME message.

RFC 6522 removes that constraint. The RFC states that no other changes apart from some editorial ones are made, and that other memos might establish or clarify constraints on using multipart/report where they are needed.
sections.eli5: The old rule said the report folder had to be the only thing in the envelope. That was too strict, so the new rule lets it be tucked inside bigger envelopes.

sections.title: The Multipart/Report Structure
sections.content:
The media type is a general family or container type for electronic mail reports of any kind. This memo defines its use only for delivery status reports, but mail processing programs benefit if a single media type is used for all kinds of reports. Its syntax is identical to multipart/mixed from RFC 2045, and both the boundary and report-type parameters are required. There are no optional parameters.

The report-type parameter names the kind of report. Its value is the MIME subtype of the second body part.

The container holds two or three sub-parts, in this order:

  • Part 1 (required): a human-readable message describing the condition that caused the report, for a reader whose mail program cannot interpret part 2. It can use any IANA-registered media type, charset or language, and a multipart/alternative construct MAY be used to offer several languages or media.
  • Part 2 (required): a machine-parsable account of the reported mail handling event. The initial body part defined for this is message/delivery-status, from RFC 3464.
  • Part 3 (optional): the returned message or a portion of it, which helps human experts diagnose problems.
sections.eli5: A report has a fixed order of pages. First a note a person can read, then a form for computers, and last, if wanted, a copy of the original letter.

sections.title: Returning the Original Message
sections.content:
Returning content can waste network bandwidth, so implementations can use different strategies. Generally the sender chooses a strategy and tells the recipient the level of returned content required. When there is no explicit request, such as the one that RFC 3461 provides, the agent that generated the report SHOULD return the full message content.

If 8-bit or binary data not encoded in a 7-bit form is to be returned, and the return path is not guaranteed to be 8-bit or binary capable, there are two options. The original message MAY be re-encoded into a legal 7-bit MIME message, or the text/rfc822-headers media type MAY be used to return only the original message headers. The RFC says 7bit should always be adequate as the encoding for multipart/report itself.
sections.eli5: Sending back the whole original letter can be heavy. By default the reporter sends all of it, but it can send just the envelope information if that is safer or lighter.

sections.title: The text/rfc822-headers Type
sections.content:
This memo also defines text/rfc822-headers, a way to label and return only the header of a failed message. The header is not the complete message, so it SHOULD NOT be returned using the message/rfc822 type from RFC 2046. It is useful for identifying the failed message and for diagnostics based on the Received header fields.

The body part SHOULD contain all the mail header fields from the message that caused the report, meaning everything before the first blank line. That includes the MIME-Version and MIME content description fields. The type has no parameters. Seven-bit encoding is enough for normal headers, but headers that are broken or extended MAY be encoded with quoted-printable.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you only need the address label from the original letter, not the letter itself. This type is for sending back just that label.

sections.title: Registering New Report Types
sections.content:
Other kinds of report can use the same container. A registration for a new media type created to be a report format SHOULD say, in the Intended Usage section of the registration, that the type is suitable for use as a report-type, that is, as the second body part.

The multipart/report registration itself says that restrictions on usage are none, but that other applications which register report types may establish such restrictions. It lists mail transfer agents, mail user agents, and spam, virus and message authentication modules as applications that use the type.
sections.eli5: If someone invents a new kind of report, they should write down that it can go in the second slot of the folder.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using report types automatically, without authentication, creates several risks. Forged negative reports can enable denial-of-service attacks when reports are used for automated maintenance of directories or mailing lists. Forged positive reports can make a sender wrongly believe a message was delivered when it was not.

A signature covering the entire multipart/report structure could prevent such forgeries, but the RFC says such a signature scheme is beyond its scope.

In its IANA section, the memo updates the Media Type Registry to say this document holds the current definition of multipart/report and text/rfc822-headers, obsoleting RFC 3462.
sections.eli5: Anyone could fake a report. A fake 'it failed' note could get you removed from a list, and a fake 'it worked' note could make you think a letter arrived when it did not.
